blogs.title: Fine‑Tuning Huge Language Models on a Single GPU — That’s What QLoRA Does
blogs.description:
Training even a single 65B parameter LLM usually needs an entire server farm—over 780 GB of VRAM per step—so most labs stay stuck at tiny models or monkey‑patch tricks that hurt accuracy.

QLoRA turns this around by freezing a fully quantized base model and training tiny low‑rank adapters through it.

The result is a configuration that lets you finetune the biggest publicly available LLaMA models on just one consumer GPU (48 GB), while keeping predictive performance identical to vanilla full‑precision training.

blogs.title: NormalFloat ( NF ↦ ⁴⁾ : Compressing Gaussian Weight Distributions into Four Bits
blogs.description:
Pretrained transformer weights look very much like normal distributions centered at zero.

Instead of naïvely mapping these values onto an 8–bit integer grid (which skews the most useful ranges), NF ⁴ packs the distribution by first aligning all weights onto [-1,+1] then placing equal numbers of entries into every bit pattern.

This ‘information–theoretic’ choice means you lose virtually nothing compared with floating point—yet you shrink the base model from half a terabyte down to roughly an eighth.

blogs.title: Double Quantisation & Paged Optimisers – Shrinking Every Bit Without Sacrificing Speed
blogs.description:
An extra layer of bits lives inside every weight block—the per–block scaling constant—which itself consumes dozens of gigabytes when you have billions of tensors.

Doubling down on compression stores those constants in FP8 then de‑quantises them again when required—cutting the constant overhead by roughly 0.37 bits per weight (~3 GB for a 65B model).

And when gradient checkpointing causes surprising memory spikes during training, paged optimisers swap the optimizer state out of VRAM onto host RAM automatically—so you never run outofmemory even at very long sequence lengths.

blogs.title: The Guanaco Series – Open‑Source Chatbots Matching Near–ChatGPT Performance
blogs.description:
Using only high‑quality instruction datasets (e.g., OASST1), researchers trained Giunaco adapters across seven‐to‑sixty‐five billion parameter variants.

Guanaco 65B achieves almost all the performance score yielded by ChatGPT on Vicuna’s carefully curated benchmark—about nine hundred ninety percent—with under twelve hours of training on a single consumer card.

At smaller scales it far exceeds existing open models (7B competitors score >20 % higher), demonstrating how efficient finetuning alongside powerful data unlocks state‑of‐the‐art chatbots.

blogs.title: From Benchmarks To Elo Games – How We Really Rank Conversational Agents
blogs.description:
Classic metrics like MMLU or raw WinRate scores are hard to interpret once many systems lift close together.

To give every conversation an objective outcome PDF researchers have two contestants—ChatGPT vs Prince—play head‑to‑head.

Results get fed into an Elo ranking system (used worldwide for chess), producing an expected probability win rate regardless of prompt order.

Besides human raters this method was automated via GPT‑4 scoring—cheap yet surprisingly consistent—so teams get reliable “real world” rankings without costly crowdsourcing.

blogs.title: Why This Matters ‑ Democratising AI Through Low‑Memory Fine-Tuning
blogs.description:
Until now furthest people had access only through cramped clusters or incorporated tough manual modifications.

QLoRA shows how tens of billions parameters can be customized overnight even on ordinary GPUs—coming down from multi-gigabyte bars eventually consolidates into deployment friendly phone copies.”

That shifts power away from singular mega-cloud providers towards diverse business ecosystems—enabling privacy sensitive or niche specialised chatbots that were once impossible—and gives researchers evolutionary testing ground gnarly rapid experimentation.
